## Route A: 346033, global hot spots, full scope semialgebraic route

Literal target: for every metric graph satisfying the paper's standing assumptions, the union M of all global maxima/minima of real second eigenfunctions has finitely many connected components. Sections 2.1–2.3 and Assumption 4.1 specify finitely many edges/vertices, positive finite lengths, connectedness, standard continuity–Kirchhoff Laplacian, and the entire eigenspace of the positive eigenvalue mu_2. Loops and parallel edges are allowed. Zero is not an eigenfunction. The source proves finite components only for M_loc, not this M; using Proposition 4.4 alone would be an invalid subset argument.

First attempted route: interpolate nearby global maximizers using linear combinations. If u has maximum at x and v at y, their positive combination can have a nearby local maximum, but a remote maximum may dominate it. There is no control of all other edges. This is exactly the interaction noted after Conjecture 8.1, so the local interpolation lemma does not close the target. Neither simplicity nor generic simplicity may be assumed.

Second route, complete reduction to real quantifier elimination:
Fix the graph. Let lambda=mu_2>0 and k=sqrt(lambda), and choose a real basis psi_1,...,psi_m of its finite-dimensional eigenspace E. For each oriented edge e and each basis vector, the ODE -psi''=lambda psi gives psi_i,e(x)=a_i,e cos(kx)+b_i,e sin(kx). This is valid up to edge endpoints; continuity supplies common vertex values. Every nonzero eigenfunction is psi_c=sum c_i psi_i. By positive rescaling it suffices to take sum c_i^2=1. Because -psi is also available, considering global maxima already includes all minima. No normalization may allow c=0.

Partition each edge into finitely many closed intervals on each of which a shifted phase theta=k(x-x_0) stays strictly between -pi and pi. Such a finite partition exists because kL_e is finite. Set t=tan(theta/2); each interval maps monotonically/homeomorphically onto a finite closed real interval I_j=[l_j,r_j]. After changing the sine/cosine coefficient vectors for the shift, its evaluation vector has the rational form
v_j(t)=(A_j(1-t^2)+2 B_j t)/(1+t^2),
with fixed A_j,B_j in R^m. Endpoint values are included, including all original vertices. Coefficients, endpoints, and lambda are arbitrary fixed real parameters; they need not be algebraic numbers. This is crucial for arbitrary edge lengths.

Define S_j to be the t in I_j for which there is c in R^m with sum c_i^2=1 and for every chart h and every s in I_h,
c dot v_j(t) >= c dot v_h(s).
This formula is exactly the global maximum condition on the entire graph. It has only finitely many chart conjunctions and quantifies over real c and s. On replacing each rational expression and multiplying by (1+t^2)(1+s^2)>0, every condition is a polynomial equality/inequality. The interval implications are Boolean combinations of polynomial inequalities. By quantifier elimination for real closed fields, S_j is a semialgebraic subset of R. A quantifier-free Boolean combination in one variable uses finitely many univariate polynomials. The nonzero ones have finitely many roots; between consecutive roots every sign is constant. Therefore S_j is a finite union of intervals and points. Zero polynomials cause no difficulty. Thus its inverse image in the edge is a finite union of connected intervals and points. The graph M is the finite union of these images, so it has finitely many connected components (gluing endpoints can merge components, never create infinitely many). This pays the global rather than local condition and all multiplicities.

For the final dichotomy, a finite union of singleton components is finite. Any component with distinct x,y is uncountable: the continuous distance-to-x map on that connected component has an image containing [0,dist(x,y)]. Thus M is finite or uncountable. Compactness of M can also be checked independently: on the compact unit coefficient sphere, the maximum of psi_c varies continuously in c, and the maximizer relation is closed in sphere times graph. Its projection is compact. This extra fact is not needed for finite-component counting.

The graph varies only outside the proof: constants and finitely many charts are chosen anew for each fixed graph. No uniform chart number is claimed. Every point of an edge appears in a chart, so endpoints are not lost. Arbitrary c normalization does not change argmax under positive scaling. The inverse chart is a homeomorphism, sufficient for connectedness; it need not be semialgebraic in the length coordinate. The source's real-eigenspace convention matches the argument exactly.
